analysis.one_liner: Strips the FCC of its power to review telecom mergers or attach conditions to licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee and died at the end of the 106th Congress without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have taken away the Federal Communications Commission's power to review mergers involving phone, cable, and broadcast companies and to attach conditions when licenses changed hands in a deal. Once the Justice Department or Federal Trade Commission looked at a merger and cleared it — or even just said they would not intervene — the FCC would have been required to approve the license transfer with no conditions of its own. If the FCC failed to act within 60 days in the rare cases it could still review, the transfer would be approved automatically.
analysis.who_benefits: Large telecommunications and media companies planning mergers. The bill would have eliminated a second layer of government review that could impose public-interest conditions — like commitments to competition, service areas, or spectrum use — when broadcast and telecom licenses changed hands in a deal. It also would have sped up approvals and removed the risk that the FCC would reject or burden a merger the antitrust agencies had already cleared.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large telecom and media companies seeking mergers

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the FCC's authority to approve telecommunications mergers under the Clayton Act and gives the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission primary authority over mergers involving communications licenses [S2][S3].

Once DOJ or the FTC approves a merger — or issues a written statement that it will not intervene — the FCC must authorize the license transfer as proposed and may not impose any term, condition, or obligation on the merging parties [S3].

The FCC could review a merger only if neither antitrust agency issued any decision or statement, and had to finish within 60 days; if it missed the deadline, the transfer would be deemed approved unconditionally by default [S2][S3].
The bill's stated findings argue that the FCC's merger review produced delay, inconsistency, and unwarranted costs on the industry [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers and communities that depend on broadcast and telecom licenses. The FCC's license-transfer review is the one place where regulators can attach public-interest conditions — such as preserving competition, service commitments, or local programming — to the transfer of a scarce public license. The bill would have removed that leverage in every merger the antitrust agencies touched, and antitrust review looks only at competitive effects, not broader public-interest goals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers and communities served by merged firms

drawbacks.text: Dual review by the FCC and the antitrust agencies did create real delay, duplication, and inconsistent decisions, and merging parties could not proceed even after DOJ or the FTC approved them, imposing costs on companies and the public [S3].

The bill would have barred the FCC from imposing any conditions on license transfers in mergers the antitrust agencies reviewed, ending the main regulatory lever for public-interest conditions on scarce broadcast and telecom licenses [S2][S3].
In the narrow window where the FCC could still review, a 60-day deadline with automatic unconditional approval would have pressured the agency to rubber-stamp transfers rather than examine them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Consolidating merger review in DOJ and the FTC has genuine efficiency appeal — the FCC's parallel review did slow deals and overlap with antitrust analysis. But the bill went further than streamlining: it forbade the FCC from attaching any public-interest conditions to license transfers and made approval automatic once the antitrust agencies acted. The savings in review time would come at the cost of the only mechanism that requires merged telecom and media companies to give anything back for the licenses they acquire.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on May 26, 1999, naming Sens. Ashcroft, Hatch, and Mack in the introduction [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1][S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the FCC kept its authority to review telecom mergers and impose conditions on license transfers. Companies hoping for faster, unconditional merger approvals did not get them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public; the FCC kept merger-review power

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-AZ); sponsor; chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the FCC of merger-review authority

for.name: Sens. John Ashcroft and Orrin Hatch

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; all of the bill's sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, but no Democrat ever had to take a position because it never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would have let telecom, cable, and broadcast companies complete mergers with no FCC conditions attached to license transfers, eliminating the regulator that could require concessions in exchange for taking over a public license. Its interest in faster, unconditional deals runs against the public's interest in conditions protecting competition and service.

industries.industry: Telecommunications law and regulatory consulting firms
industries.note: Removing FCC merger review would eliminate a large volume of FCC merger-application work, while consolidating more of the process at DOJ and the FTC. This is a secondary, modest effect.
